questions.prompt: In fish liver oil there is:
questions.explanation: Fish liver oil (e.g. cod liver oil) is a rich source of both fat-soluble vitamins A and D.

questions.prompt: When day and night are equal?
questions.explanation: Day and night are (nearly) equal at the equinoxes, around 21 March (vernal) and 23 September (autumnal).

questions.prompt: The chemical formula for alum is:
questions.explanation: Potash alum is potassium aluminium sulphate dodecahydrate, KAl(SO4)2·12H2O.

questions.prompt: One degree of longitude on the equator is equal to a distance of:
questions.explanation: Earth's equatorial circumference ≈ 24,901 miles; ÷ 360 ≈ 69.2 miles (about 111 km) per degree of longitude at the equator.

questions.prompt: The protein molecule is made of:
options: Short range chain of amino acids
Long range chain of amino acids
questions.explanation: Proteins are long polypeptide chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; short chains are just peptides.

questions.prompt: The minimum amount of vitamin stored in the human body is of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is water-soluble, so excess is excreted in urine and very little is stored; A, D and E are fat-soluble and stored in liver/fat.

questions.prompt: The pH of soil is raised using:
questions.explanation: Agricultural lime (limestone, CaCO3) neutralises soil acidity and raises pH; gypsum is used to reclaim sodic soils without raising pH.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is used for measuring distance?
questions.explanation: A light year is the distance light travels in one year (≈9.46 × 10^12 km); coulomb, farad and curie are units of charge, capacitance and radioactivity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following contains a greater number of carbon atoms in one mole of each compound?
questions.explanation: Ethanol (C2H5OH) has 2 carbon atoms per molecule; chloroform (CHCl3) and methanol (CH3OH) have 1 and water has none.

questions.prompt: A pencil dipped in water appears bent due to:
questions.explanation: Light bends (refracts) as it passes from water to air, so the submerged part appears displaced and the pencil looks bent.

questions.prompt: Fishes die outside the water due to:
questions.explanation: Out of water, gill filaments collapse and dry out, so fish cannot absorb oxygen and suffocate.

questions.prompt: In dementia a person:
questions.explanation: Dementia is the loss of cognitive functioning: thinking, remembering and reasoning, severe enough to interfere with daily life.

questions.prompt: Earthquake is measured by the instrument:
questions.explanation: A seismograph records seismic waves; a barometer measures air pressure and a hydrometer liquid density.

questions.prompt: A cyclone is formed:
options: When the warm air rises upward over the ocean
When moist air rises upward over the ocean
When moist air pressed downward over the ocean
When warm, moist air rises upward over the ocean
questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones form when warm, moist air over warm ocean water rises, creating low pressure; condensation releases heat that fuels the storm.

questions.prompt: Why red light is used in traffic signal for danger?
options: It has long wavelength and high frequency
It has long wavelength and short frequency
questions.explanation: Red has the longest wavelength (lowest frequency) of visible light, so it is scattered least and can be seen from the farthest distance.

questions.prompt: The heavy water is:
options: Denoted by D2O and contains simple hydrogen
Denoted by H2O and contains deuterium
Denoted by D2O and contains deuterium
Denoted by H2O and contains simple hydrogen
questions.explanation: Heavy water is D2O, deuterium oxide, in which hydrogen is replaced by its isotope deuterium (one proton + one neutron).

questions.prompt: Which of the following source of energy is caused by uneven heating of earth’s surface?
questions.explanation: Uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the sun creates pressure differences, which drive winds; wind energy is thus an indirect form of solar energy.

questions.prompt: Global winds towards western direction are known as:
questions.explanation: Trade winds (tropical easterlies) blow from east towards the west between about 30°N and 30°S; westerlies blow the other way, from west to east.

questions.prompt: Perinatal transmission is said to occur when a pathogen is transmitted from:
questions.explanation: Perinatal (vertical) transmission passes an infection from mother to baby around the time of birth, e.g. hepatitis B or HIV.

questions.prompt: Which of the plant group needs both land and water to complete their life cycle?
questions.explanation: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) live on land but need water for their sperm to swim to the egg, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

questions.prompt: Maximum amount of carbohydrates are obtained from:
questions.explanation: Whole grains (wheat, rice, maize) are mostly starch; nuts are rich in fat and protein and plant oils are almost pure fat.

questions.prompt: Which of the following class has the largest number of animals?
questions.explanation: Insects (class Insecta) are the largest class of animals, with about a million described species, far more than fishes or mammals.

questions.prompt: The process of preserving meat by stewing in a covered earthenware jug is called:
questions.explanation: Jugging is stewing meat (traditionally hare or game) slowly in a tightly covered earthenware jug or casserole, which also helped preserve it.

questions.prompt: The amount of data transmitted for a given amount of time is called:
questions.explanation: In networking, bandwidth is the amount of data that can be carried per unit time, measured in bits per second.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is used as a stabilizer in ice cream?
questions.explanation: Gelatin (like guar gum or carrageenan) is a stabilizer: it binds water and stops large ice crystals forming, keeping ice cream smooth.

questions.prompt: In the structure of fiber, the light is guided through the core due to total internal:
questions.explanation: Light stays in an optical fibre core by total internal reflection, because the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding.

questions.prompt: Who is known as the inventor of Artificial Intelligence?
questions.explanation: John McCarthy coined the term 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and is called the father of AI; Turing proposed the earlier 'Turing test' (1950).

questions.prompt: The fastest enzyme is:
questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase is among the fastest enzymes, converting up to about a million CO2 molecules per second (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3).

questions.prompt: Process of adding vitamins to milk is known as:
questions.explanation: Fortification is adding micronutrients (e.g. vitamins A and D) to foods such as milk, flour or salt.

questions.prompt: The waves which are used for line of sight (LOS) communication are called:
questions.explanation: Space waves (VHF/UHF/microwave) travel in straight lines from transmitter to receiver, i.e. line-of-sight propagation, as in TV, mobile and satellite links.

questions.prompt: Rapid short-term weather changes are most strongly influenced by:
questions.explanation: Day-to-day weather is driven by moving high- and low-pressure systems and fronts; revolution and precession act over seasons or millennia.

questions.prompt: The primary structure of a protein is determined by its:
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids; hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges shape secondary/tertiary structure.

questions.prompt: In plants, lignin primarily provides:
questions.explanation: Lignin is a rigid polymer in the cell walls of wood and xylem that gives plants mechanical strength and support.

questions.prompt: The Montreal Protocol focuses on the reduction of:
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs and halons; CO2 is dealt with by the UNFCCC/Paris Agreement.

questions.prompt: A key indicator of drinking water microbiological safety is:
questions.explanation: E. coli indicates faecal contamination; WHO guidelines require none detectable in 100 mL of drinking water.

questions.prompt: Bioavailability of nutrients in food refers to:
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is the proportion of a nutrient that is absorbed and used by the body.

questions.prompt: A CPU’s instruction cycle primarily depends on ____________ for coordinating all operations.
questions.explanation: The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and directs the ALU, memory and I/O during the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

questions.prompt: The protocol responsible for mapping domain names to IP addresses in global internet architecture is:
questions.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates names like fpsc.gov.pk into IP addresses; DHCP assigns IPs and ARP maps IP to MAC addresses.

questions.prompt: Knowledge graphs enhance AI reasoning capabilities by representing data as:
questions.explanation: A knowledge graph stores entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, which lets AI systems reason over connections.

questions.prompt: Wind turbines convert which form of energy directly into electricity?
questions.explanation: Wind turbines capture the kinetic energy of moving air; the rotor turns a generator that produces electricity.

questions.prompt: LEDs save energy because light is produced by:
questions.explanation: In an LED, electrons recombine with holes at a p-n junction and release energy as photons (electroluminescence), wasting little as heat, unlike filament bulbs.

questions.prompt: The major storage lipid in animals is:
questions.explanation: Animals store fat as triglycerides in adipose tissue; glycogen is a stored carbohydrate, not a lipid.

questions.prompt: Acid Rain primarily results from emissions of:
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react with water in the air to form sulphuric and nitric acids, which fall as acid rain.

questions.prompt: A major global impact of particulate matter (PM2.5) is:
questions.explanation: PM2.5 particles (≤2.5 µm) penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and heart disease; a main component of smog.

questions.prompt: Heavy metal contamination (e.g. mercury) is most harmful because it:
questions.explanation: Heavy metals like mercury are not broken down, so they accumulate and become more concentrated at each level of the food chain (biomagnification).

questions.prompt: Fiber optic cables support high bandwidth communication because data travels as:
questions.explanation: Optical fibres carry data as pulses of light with very low loss and very high frequency, giving far higher bandwidth than copper cables.

questions.prompt: Remote sensing is primarily used in environmental studies to:
questions.explanation: Remote sensing gathers data about large areas of the Earth from satellites or aircraft without physical contact.

questions.prompt: A Decision Support System (DSS) differs from routine MIS primarily by providing:
questions.explanation: An MIS produces routine reports for structured decisions; a DSS supports semi-structured/unstructured decisions with models and what-if analysis.

questions.prompt: Satellite communication signals suffer from significant latency mainly due to:
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite is ~35,786 km up, so a signal going up and down takes roughly 0.25 s one way, causing noticeable delay.

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²); the joule is energy, the pascal pressure and the watt power.

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω); by Ohm's law R = V/I.

questions.prompt: Sound cannot travel through which of the following?
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.prompt: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids (about 5,900 m/s in steel), slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

questions.prompt: The approximate speed of light in a vacuum is:
questions.explanation: Light travels at about 300,000 km/s (3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum; 343 m/s is the speed of sound in air at 20 °C.

questions.prompt: A body's mass is 60 kg on Earth. What is its mass on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location; only weight (mg) changes, being about one-sixth on the Moon.

questions.prompt: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Red light has the longest wavelength (about 700 nm) and violet the shortest (about 400 nm) in the visible spectrum.

questions.prompt: The blue colour of the clear daytime sky is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Air molecules scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths much more than longer ones (Rayleigh scattering), so the sky looks blue.

questions.prompt: A spoon dipped in a glass of water looks bent at the surface because of:
questions.explanation: Light bends (refracts) as it passes from water to air, so the submerged part of the spoon appears displaced.

questions.prompt: Which type of lens is used to correct short-sightedness (myopia)?
questions.explanation: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens moves it back onto the retina.

questions.prompt: Newton's third law of motion states that:
options: A body stays at rest unless acted on by a force
To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
Momentum is always conserved in collisions only
questions.explanation: The third law pairs forces: action and reaction are equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on different bodies.

questions.prompt: The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or motion is called:
questions.explanation: Inertia, described by Newton's first law, depends on mass.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Speed has magnitude only; velocity, acceleration and force also have direction, so they are vectors.

questions.prompt: One kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of:
questions.explanation: 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in one hour, equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ joules.

questions.prompt: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same reading?
questions.explanation: Setting C = F in F = 9C/5 + 32 gives C = −40, so −40 °C = −40 °F.

questions.prompt: Why does water boil at a lower temperature at high altitudes?
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure; lower air pressure at altitude means this is reached at a lower temperature.

questions.prompt: Which electromagnetic radiation has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: In order of decreasing wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

questions.prompt: A fuse in an electric circuit works on the principle of:
questions.explanation: Excess current heats the fuse wire (of low melting point) until it melts and breaks the circuit.

questions.prompt: An electric generator works on the principle of:
questions.explanation: Generators convert mechanical energy into electrical energy by Faraday's electromagnetic induction; a changing magnetic flux induces an emf.

questions.prompt: A transformer works only with:
questions.explanation: A transformer needs a changing magnetic flux to induce voltage in the secondary coil, which only alternating current provides.

questions.prompt: Echoes are clearly heard only when the reflecting surface is at least about how far away in air (taking sound speed 340 m/s and persistence of hearing 0.1 s)?
questions.explanation: Sound must travel to the wall and back (2d) in at least 0.1 s: 2d = 340 × 0.1 = 34 m, so d = 17 m.

questions.prompt: Sound waves of frequency above 20,000 Hz are called:
questions.explanation: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; above it is ultrasound (used in medical scans), below it infrasound.

questions.prompt: The device that converts alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC) is called a:
questions.explanation: A rectifier (usually made of diodes) converts AC to DC; an inverter converts DC to AC.

questions.prompt: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which statement is correct?
options: Its velocity changes continuously, so it is accelerating
Its velocity is constant because its speed is constant
Its acceleration points away from the centre
questions.explanation: Direction of motion changes continuously, so velocity changes; the (centripetal) acceleration points towards the centre.

questions.prompt: What is the chemical formula of common table salt?
questions.explanation: Table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl; NaHCO₃ is baking soda.

questions.prompt: Which gas is most abundant in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: The pH of pure water at 25 °C is:
questions.explanation: Pure water is neutral with pH 7; below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the hardest natural substance?
questions.explanation: Diamond, a form of carbon in which each atom bonds to four others in a rigid 3-D lattice, is the hardest natural material.

questions.prompt: Graphite and diamond are both forms of:
questions.explanation: Different structural forms of the same element are allotropes; graphite, diamond and fullerenes are allotropes of carbon.

questions.prompt: The chemical name of baking soda is:
questions.explanation: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate (bicarbonate), NaHCO₃; sodium carbonate is washing soda.

questions.prompt: Which gas is known as 'laughing gas'?
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide (N₂O) produces euphoria and is used as an anaesthetic.

questions.prompt: Rusting of iron requires:
questions.explanation: Rust (hydrated iron(III) oxide) forms only when iron is exposed to both oxygen and moisture.

questions.prompt: Coating iron with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting is called:
questions.explanation: Galvanising protects iron with zinc; vulcanisation is the hardening of rubber with sulphur.

questions.prompt: Which is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury melts at about −39 °C; gallium melts at about 30 °C, just above normal room temperature.

questions.prompt: The atomic number of an element equals the number of:
questions.explanation: Atomic number (Z) is the proton count; mass number is protons plus neutrons.

questions.prompt: Isotopes of an element differ in their number of:
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, hence different mass numbers.

questions.prompt: Which gas is used in electric bulbs to prolong filament life?
questions.explanation: An inert gas such as argon (sometimes with nitrogen) prevents the hot tungsten filament from oxidising.

questions.prompt: Which element has the chemical symbol 'Fe'?
questions.explanation: Fe comes from the Latin 'ferrum'; lead is Pb, fluorine F and francium Fr.

questions.prompt: The acid present in the human stomach is:
questions.explanation: Gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, which aids digestion and kills microbes.

questions.prompt: An acid reacts with a base to form salt and water. This reaction is called:
questions.explanation: Acid + base → salt + water is neutralisation; saponification is the making of soap from fats and alkali.

questions.prompt: Which gas turns lime water milky?
questions.explanation: CO₂ reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which makes lime water cloudy.

questions.prompt: Noble gases are chemically unreactive mainly because they have:
questions.explanation: A complete valence shell (duplet for helium, octet for the others) makes noble gases very stable.

questions.prompt: LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) used in cylinders is mainly a mixture of:
questions.explanation: LPG is chiefly propane and butane; natural gas (CNG) is mainly methane.

questions.prompt: CNG used in vehicles consists mainly of:
questions.explanation: Compressed natural gas is mostly methane (CH₄) stored under high pressure.

questions.prompt: Which organ pumps blood throughout the human body?
questions.explanation: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.

questions.prompt: Which blood cells help the body fight infection?
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leucocytes) defend the body; red cells carry oxygen and platelets help clotting.

questions.prompt: The pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen is:
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.

questions.prompt: Which blood group is called the 'universal donor'?
questions.explanation: O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh(D) antigens, so they can be given to recipients of any ABO/Rh group in emergencies.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation: The skin is the largest organ by surface area and weight; the liver is the largest internal organ.

questions.prompt: Insulin is produced by the:
questions.explanation: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose.

questions.prompt: Deficiency of vitamin D in children causes:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium; deficiency weakens bones, causing rickets in children.

questions.prompt: Night blindness is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin A forms rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment in rod cells of the retina.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin is essential for normal blood clotting?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is needed to make several clotting factors in the liver.

questions.prompt: Goitre is caused mainly by a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones; deficiency makes the gland enlarge (goitre).

questions.prompt: Iron deficiency in the diet commonly causes:
questions.explanation: Iron is needed for haemoglobin; deficiency causes iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.prompt: Malaria is transmitted by the bite of the female:
questions.explanation: Plasmodium parasites are spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes; Aedes spreads dengue.

questions.prompt: Dengue fever is spread by the:
questions.explanation: Aedes aegypti (and Aedes albopictus), which bite mainly in the daytime, transmit the dengue virus.

questions.prompt: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.explanation: Polio is caused by poliovirus; tuberculosis, typhoid and cholera are bacterial.

questions.prompt: Tuberculosis is caused by a:
questions.explanation: TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mainly affects the lungs.

questions.prompt: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explanation: Each kidney has about a million nephrons that filter blood and form urine.

questions.prompt: Gas exchange in human lungs takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Alveoli are tiny air sacs with thin walls surrounded by capillaries, where O₂ and CO₂ are exchanged.

questions.prompt: Most digestion and absorption of food takes place in the:
questions.explanation: The small intestine, with its villi, completes digestion and absorbs most nutrients; the large intestine absorbs mainly water.

questions.prompt: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the:
questions.explanation: Bile, which emulsifies fats, is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder.

questions.prompt: How many bones are there in an adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: An adult has 206 bones; a newborn has around 270–300, many of which fuse with age.

questions.prompt: The smallest bone in the human body is the:
questions.explanation: The stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear is the smallest bone; the femur is the longest.

questions.prompt: The normal human body temperature is about:
questions.explanation: Normal core temperature is about 37 °C (98.6 °F).

questions.prompt: The normal resting blood pressure of a healthy adult is usually taken as about:
questions.explanation: Systolic about 120 and diastolic about 80 mmHg is the conventional normal value.

questions.prompt: Which part of the human brain controls balance and coordination of movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and balance; the medulla controls breathing and heart rate.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions such as breathing and heartbeat?
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata in the brainstem regulates vital autonomic functions.

questions.prompt: Which gland is called the 'master gland' of the endocrine system?
questions.explanation: The pituitary secretes hormones that control several other endocrine glands.

questions.prompt: Penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, was discovered by:
questions.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928; Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine and Pasteur the rabies vaccine.

questions.prompt: Antibiotics are effective against infections caused by:
questions.explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes; they do not work against viruses such as those causing colds and flu.

questions.prompt: Plants make their food by the process of:
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and release oxygen.

questions.prompt: The 'powerhouse of the cell', where aerobic respiration releases energy, is the:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP; ribosomes make proteins.

questions.prompt: Loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants is called:
questions.explanation: Transpiration occurs mainly through stomata and helps pull water up the plant.

questions.prompt: DNA in eukaryotic cells is found mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Most DNA is in the nucleus, with small amounts in mitochondria (and chloroplasts in plants).

questions.prompt: A normal human body cell contains how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Human somatic cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); gametes have 23.

questions.prompt: The layer of the atmosphere closest to Earth's surface, where weather occurs, is the:
questions.explanation: The troposphere extends to about 8–18 km and contains most water vapour and weather.

questions.prompt: The ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, lies mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Most ozone is in the stratosphere, roughly 15–35 km above the surface.

questions.prompt: Depletion of the ozone layer has been caused mainly by:
questions.explanation: CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere that destroys ozone; the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased them out.

questions.prompt: Which gas is the largest contributor to human-caused global warming?
questions.explanation: CO₂ from burning fossil fuels and deforestation is the main anthropogenic greenhouse gas; methane is second.

questions.prompt: Acid rain is caused mainly by emissions of:
questions.explanation: SO₂ and NOₓ dissolve in rainwater to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

questions.prompt: The outermost solid layer of the Earth is called the:
questions.explanation: Earth's layers from outside in: crust, mantle, outer core (liquid), inner core (solid).

questions.prompt: The scale commonly used to report the magnitude of an earthquake is the:
questions.explanation: Earthquake magnitude is given on the Richter/moment magnitude scale; Beaufort measures wind and Mohs mineral hardness.

questions.prompt: The point on Earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake is the:
questions.explanation: The focus (hypocentre) is underground where rupture begins; the epicentre is directly above it.

questions.prompt: Large sea waves caused by undersea earthquakes are called:
questions.explanation: A tsunami is a series of waves triggered by sudden displacement of the seabed.

questions.prompt: Rocks formed by the cooling and solidification of magma are called:
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks (e.g. granite, basalt) form from molten magma; sedimentary rocks form from deposited layers.

questions.prompt: The main cause of tides in the oceans is the gravitational pull of the:
questions.explanation: The Moon's gravity is the main cause of tides; the Sun contributes a smaller effect.

questions.prompt: The international agreement adopted in 2015 to limit global warming to well below 2 °C is the:
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015) aims to hold warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C.

questions.prompt: The process by which bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds usable by plants is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g. Rhizobium in legume root nodules) convert N₂ into ammonia.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-biodegradable material?
questions.explanation: Polythene is not broken down by microorganisms in a reasonable time, so it persists as waste.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest planet in our Solar System?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the largest planet, with more than 300 times Earth's mass.

questions.prompt: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

questions.prompt: Which is the hottest planet in the Solar System?
questions.explanation: Venus's thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat (runaway greenhouse effect), making it hotter than Mercury.

questions.prompt: Light from the Sun takes approximately how long to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: At about 150 million km, sunlight takes roughly 500 seconds (8 min 20 s) to arrive.

questions.prompt: A light-year is a unit of:
questions.explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹² km.

questions.prompt: A solar eclipse occurs when the:
options: Moon comes between the Sun and Earth
Moon is in its full phase
Sun comes between Earth and Moon
Earth comes between the Sun and Moon
questions.explanation: In a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on Earth; a lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the most prominent ring system?
questions.explanation: All four giant planets have rings, but Saturn's are by far the largest and brightest.

questions.prompt: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a:
questions.explanation: The IAU's 2006 definition reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood.

questions.prompt: The galaxy that contains our Solar System is the:
questions.explanation: The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.

questions.prompt: Pakistan's first satellite, launched in 1990, was:
questions.explanation: Badr-1 was launched on 16 July 1990 from China; PRSS-1 (2018) was Pakistan's first remote-sensing satellite.

questions.prompt: CPU stands for:
questions.explanation: The CPU executes instructions and is often called the brain of the computer.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an input device?
questions.explanation: A keyboard sends data into the computer; monitors, printers and speakers are output devices.

questions.prompt: One byte is equal to:
questions.explanation: A byte is 8 bits; a kilobyte is conventionally 1,024 bytes in binary usage.

questions.prompt: Which type of memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile working memory; ROM, hard disks and flash storage are non-volatile.

questions.prompt: The binary number 1011 is equal to which decimal number?
HTTP stands for:
questions.explanation: HTTP is the protocol used to transfer web pages; HTTPS is its encrypted form.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an operating system?
questions.explanation: Linux is an operating system kernel; Word is an application, Chrome a browser and Oracle a database system.

questions.prompt: A computer program that replicates itself and spreads by attaching to other files is a:
questions.explanation: A virus attaches to host files and spreads when they run; a firewall filters network traffic.

questions.prompt: A security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic is called a:
questions.explanation: A firewall applies rules to allow or block traffic between networks.

questions.prompt: A fraudulent email that tricks users into revealing passwords or bank details is an example of:
questions.explanation: Phishing uses fake messages or websites that imitate trusted organisations to steal credentials.

questions.prompt: Software whose source code is freely available to use, study and modify is called:
questions.explanation: Open-source licences allow access to and modification of source code; Linux is a well-known example.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation: Solar, wind and hydro energy are replenished naturally; fossil fuels are finite.

questions.prompt: In a nuclear power plant, energy is produced mainly by:
questions.explanation: Reactors split heavy nuclei such as uranium-235 (fission), releasing heat to make steam.

questions.prompt: The Sun produces its energy by:
questions.explanation: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing enormous energy.

questions.prompt: A solar cell (photovoltaic cell) converts:
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells, usually made of silicon, convert sunlight directly into electricity.

questions.prompt: Hydroelectric power stations convert the energy of falling water first into:
questions.explanation: The potential energy of stored water turns turbines, whose motion drives generators.

questions.prompt: The law of conservation of energy states that energy:
options: Can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another
Can be created from mass only in chemical reactions
Is always lost as heat in every process
Is conserved only in closed mechanical systems at rest
questions.explanation: The total energy of an isolated system remains constant; it is only converted between forms.

questions.prompt: Which fuel is mainly obtained from the decomposition of animal dung and plant waste?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic digestion of organic waste yields biogas, which is mostly methane.

questions.prompt: Which of these energy sources uses heat from inside the Earth?
questions.explanation: Geothermal energy taps the Earth's internal heat, e.g. hot springs and steam reservoirs.
